chapter-one.title: Chapter One: Three Traditions, One Shared Name

one-name-not-one-style.title: The First Mistake I Made
one-name-not-one-style.body:
At first, I used the word _Chhau_ as though it named one style.

It does not.

Chhau is a shared name for three regional traditions:

- Mayurbhanj Chhau, centred in Mayurbhanj district in Odisha.
- Seraikella Chhau, centred in and around Seraikella in Jharkhand.
- Purulia Chhau, practised across Purulia district in West Bengal. [1][2]

The three traditions grew in neighbouring parts of eastern India. They share connections with martial exercise, seasonal festivals, drums and reed instruments, mythological and local stories, and movement that asks a great deal from the body. [1][2]

But they do not organise those elements in the same way.

Mayurbhanj is performed without a mask. Seraikella and Purulia use masks, but their masks differ in scale, construction, and relationship to the moving body. Musical ensembles overlap but are not identical. Training words shift between regions and lineages. A similar character can enter, stand, travel, and respond to rhythm differently.

The shared name is the beginning of the investigation, not the final definition.

meeting-the-three-traditions.title: Meet Mayurbhanj, Seraikella, and Purulia
meeting-the-three-traditions.body:
**Mayurbhanj Chhau** is the unmasked tradition. The audience can see the dancer’s eyes and face, but expression does not sit there alone. Stance, torso, rhythm, direction, stillness, and relationships between performers carry the phrase. Some technical writing even describes the face as controlled or mask-like. [4][5][6]

**Seraikella Chhau** uses masks with fixed expressions. The face cannot change, so the dancer changes our reading of it. A tilt of the head, a curve in the torso, a hand placed near the mask, or a pause held slightly longer can make the same carved face appear proud, doubtful, distant, or attentive. [5]

**Purulia Chhau** is widely recognised for bold masks, large crowns, powerful music, broad pathways, dramatic conflict, turns, leaps, and acrobatic action. Its scale makes sense in relation to costume, story, open festival grounds, and a large audience. Spectacle is part of the form, but spectacle is not the same as lack of technique. [8]

I find it useful to think of the three traditions as three complete expressive systems. None is an incomplete version of another.

> Compare: Watch one entrance from each tradition. Ignore the story for the first viewing. Compare only weight, tempo, direction, scale, and the relationship between head and torso.

related-not-identical.title: How Can They Be Related and Different?
related-not-identical.body:
Mayurbhanj, Seraikella, and Purulia sit close to one another. Dancers, teachers, musicians, patrons, makers, and ideas have crossed regional boundaries for generations. Contact is not surprising. [2][3][8]

But contact does not erase local authorship.

Easy summaries often reduce the traditions to three labels: unmasked, small mask, large mask; court, court, village; vigorous, lyrical, spectacular. Those contrasts help a beginner remember the first difference. They become misleading when they are treated as full definitions.

Mayurbhanj and Seraikella both received princely patronage, but neither existed only inside a palace. Purulia has strong community and troupe networks, along with histories of patronage, public institutions, tourism, festivals, state support, and national and international stages. Seraikella can be forceful. Purulia can be still. Mayurbhanj can communicate without exaggerating the visible face. [3][8][9]

To recognise a tradition, compare a combination of choices:

- how weight enters the ground
- how a character arrives
- how movement answers rhythm
- how the face or mask is presented
- how costume changes the silhouette
- how the story fits the performance space
- how teachers pass movement from one body to another

Related and identical are not the same word.
